paragraphs: Inference in a probabilistic model means working out what its hidden variables imply after observations are available. This paper introduces an algorithmic framework that brings together variational approximation and sampling. It applies the framework to latent Dirichlet allocation and evaluates it on a challenging inference problem in population genetics.

Variational methods approach inference through an approximating distribution. The proposed framework follows that approach without restricting the approximation to the tractable distribution families used by methods such as mean field and expectation propagation. It can also be understood as sequential Monte Carlo, while removing the need to manually construct an artificial sequence of intermediate distributions.

The central contribution is a principled trade between two sources of error: variability in importance sampling estimates and bias from variational approximation. This provides a way to balance sampling and approximation within one framework. In the reported population genetics experiments, the method improves stability and accuracy over existing methods at comparable computational cost.
neurips-2009-a-stochastic-approximation-.tldr: A unified inference framework trades sampling variance against variational bias and improves stability and accuracy in reported population genetics experiments.

paragraphs: A latent factor model describes objects through hidden properties that can be shared across objects. The Indian Buffet Process provides a Bayesian way to allow an unbounded collection of such factors. This paper extends that framework to a hierarchy containing two or more layers, with each layer allowing an unbounded number of latent factors.

The layers connect through a noisy-or mechanism. Higher-level factors influence whether binary factors in the layer below are active, allowing multiple potential contributors to an activation. Conditional on the higher layer, the distribution over the lower layer factors separates into individual components. The hierarchy therefore specifies how one collection of hidden properties generates another.

The contribution is a structured extension of the latent factor representation: hidden factors can themselves have latent explanations at a higher level. The authors explore the model through a digit recognition study and an experiment involving music tags. These studies examine its properties in two application settings; the abstract does not claim a particular comparative performance advantage.
neurips-2009-an-infinite-factor-model-hi.tldr: The paper extends unbounded latent factor models into multiple layers connected by a noisy-or mechanism.

paragraphs: This paper adapts the Gamma-Poisson latent variable model to advertisement targeting in sponsored search and behaviorally targeted display advertising. Its aim is to learn useful predictive structure from click-through data at very large scale. It also addresses positional bias, where an advertisement's placement affects clicks, through a factorization with one latent dimension.

The implementation exploits both the algorithm's scaling properties and the structure of advertising data, including sparsity and locality. The authors process terabytes of data involving hundreds of millions of users and hundreds of thousands of features. Their sponsored search and display advertising implementations illustrate two different approaches to scaling the learning computation.

On Yahoo datasets, the authors report substantially better prediction accuracy than the comparison methods. For behavioral targeting, Gamma-Poisson achieves an ROC area above 0.95, compared with 0.83 for a prior Poisson regression approach. They also compare a sparse single-machine implementation with Hadoop MapReduce. The abstract describes that computational comparison as counterintuitive, without specifying which implementation wins.
neurips-2009-factor-modeling-for-adverti.tldr: Gamma-Poisson factor models improve reported ad prediction accuracy while scaling to massive sponsored search and display advertising datasets.

paragraphs: Learning an object's appearance from web images starts with a deceptively difficult problem: the object's name may have several meanings. Images associated with an abstract meaning can enter the training collection even when the desired category is a physical object. This paper develops an unsupervised method for selecting images associated with concrete senses of a category name.

The method takes only the object category's name as input and uses an online ontology to distinguish its senses. It combines image features with accompanying text to connect latent topics to particular meanings. This addresses a weakness of visual clustering alone: a visually consistent group of images does not necessarily correspond to the intended physical object.

The authors report concrete-sense retrieval results on two multimodal databases containing multiple word senses. They also experiment with classifiers trained on the selected images for ten common office objects. The approach makes semantic filtering part of collecting visual training data, using both textual and visual evidence without requiring human supervision.
neurips-2009-filtering-abstract-senses-f.tldr: An unsupervised method combines images, text, and word senses to select concrete-object images from ambiguous search results.

paragraphs: Regularization controls how strongly a learning method favors some solutions over others. This paper derives a convex objective with a Kullback-Leibler, or KL, regularization term from a PAC-Bayes risk bound. The construction uses convex losses for a stochastic Gibbs classifier that upper-bound the zero-one loss associated with a weighted majority vote.

The authors restrict the candidate posterior distributions to a family they call quasi uniform. Within that family, they propose a simple coordinate descent algorithm for minimizing the resulting objective. This connects a statistical guarantee to a concrete learning procedure: the bound motivates the cost function, and the posterior restriction makes a particular optimization strategy available.

The paper also shows that familiar objectives, including ridge regression and regularized boosting, arise by relaxing the KL divergence between a quasi uniform posterior and a uniform prior. This gives those penalties a common interpretation. In numerical experiments, the proposed algorithm generally outperforms ridge regression and AdaBoost, a qualified empirical result rather than a universal ranking.
neurips-2009-from-pac-bayes-bounds-to-kl.tldr: The paper derives KL-regularized learning from PAC-Bayes bounds and connects familiar regularizers to relaxations of that objective.

paragraphs: Neighbor embedding methods build visual representations of data by arranging points according to similarity. This paper introduces Heavy-tailed Symmetric Stochastic Neighbor Embedding, or HSSNE, which generalizes t-SNE beyond its particular Student t-distribution. The goal is to support different heavy-tailed similarity functions while also providing a practical way to optimize the resulting embedding.

The authors characterize these similarity functions using their negative score functions and introduce a parameterized family for selecting tail heaviness. They separately develop a fixed-point optimization algorithm that applies across the heavy-tailed functions and requires no user-set optimization parameters. This removes the need to tune quantities such as step size and momentum for that algorithm.

Two empirical studies examine different visualization settings. For unsupervised visualization, the optimizer is reported to match the speed and quality of the best known t-SNE implementation. For semi-supervised visualization, HSSNE performs better on the homogeneity measure and produces qualitatively better cluster separation. The claimed improvement therefore differs across the two settings.
neurips-2009-heavy-tailed-symmetric-stoc.tldr: HSSNE generalizes t-SNE's similarity functions and provides a fixed-point optimizer without user-set optimization parameters.

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm's performance tells us how efficiently one method can solve a problem. A lower bound asks a different question: how much work must any method require under a specified model of computation? This paper studies that fundamental difficulty for stochastic convex optimization, motivated by its widespread use in learning and statistical estimation.

The analysis uses an oracle model, in which an algorithm obtains information about the optimization problem through queries. Information-theoretic lower bounds constrain what an algorithm can accomplish from the information available through those interactions. This makes the computational model part of the claim: the results describe difficulty within that framework.

The authors improve existing results and obtain tight minimax complexity estimates for some function classes. Tightness means that the lower and achievable complexity estimates align in the relevant sense for those classes. These results help distinguish room for better algorithms from barriers inherent to the problem formulation, with implications for large-scale learning and estimation.
neurips-2009-information-theoretic-lower.tldr: Information-theoretic analysis establishes improved lower bounds and tight minimax complexity estimates for some stochastic convex optimization classes.

paragraphs: Bayesian nonparametric models offer flexible representations whose size need not be fixed in advance. That flexibility can make inference computationally demanding, especially when it involves averaging over many possible hidden configurations. This paper focuses on scaling inference for models based on the Indian Buffet Process, where the representation can be potentially unbounded.

The method partitions a large dataset across multiple processors. Each processor participates in likelihood computation and exchanges messages carrying statistics about the overall Bayesian posterior. These operations proceed asynchronously in a distributed system. The shared posterior statistics connect the local computations to the global inference problem, so dividing the data remains part of one coordinated sampler.

The resulting method is a new Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler, presented as the first parallel inference scheme for Indian Buffet Process models. The authors report that it supports datasets orders of magnitude larger than previously possible. Its contribution is therefore a computational route to applying flexible Bayesian representations at substantially greater data scale.
neurips-2009-large-scale-nonparametric-b.tldr: An asynchronous distributed sampler scales Indian Buffet Process inference to datasets orders of magnitude larger than previously possible.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor methods use nearby examples to help predict an input's label. This paper considers a setting with many possible labels that share underlying structure. Its objective is to estimate the probability of each label given an input, so the prediction expresses uncertainty as well as identifying plausible categories.

The proposed method learns error-correcting output codes that represent similarities among labels. These learned representations are combined with nearest-neighbor information to produce conditional probability estimates. The key idea is to incorporate relationships between output categories into a method that also uses proximity among examples. This gives label structure a direct role in the probability estimation process.

The authors apply the estimates to acoustic modeling for speech recognition. On a lecture recognition task, they report a word error rate reduction of 0.9 percentage points, equivalent to a 2.5% relative reduction, against a state-of-the-art Gaussian mixture model baseline. The result demonstrates a benefit for the reported speech task from combining learned label relationships with neighborhood information.
neurips-2009-learning-label-embeddings-f.tldr: Learned label codes improve nearest-neighbor probability estimates and reduce word error rate in a lecture recognition task.

paragraphs: Many learning procedures repeatedly compare pairs of points. Finding neighbors for every point and summing kernel contributions are two important examples, appearing in manifold learning, density estimation, and kernel methods. This paper studies how to perform these computations efficiently, along with the related scientific problem of calculating N-body potentials.

The proposed algorithms use the cover tree data structure. They address the general bichromatic setting, where the two sides of a pairwise computation can come from different collections of points. This broadens the scope beyond comparing a single dataset with itself and places several seemingly different computational tasks within the same algorithmic treatment.

The central theoretical result is a worst-case runtime of O(N) for the practical algorithms studied, presented as a first for these problems. Linear runtime means that the dependence on N grows proportionally rather than quadratically in the stated analysis. The significance is that a computation defined through pairwise relationships can admit algorithms whose analyzed runtime avoids explicitly paying for every possible pair.
neurips-2009-linear-time-algorithms-for-.tldr: Cover-tree algorithms receive linear worst-case runtime results for nearest-neighbor, kernel summation, and N-body computations.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from a subset of its entries. Earlier theoretical results discussed in this paper assume uniformly random observations, while many real datasets have highly uneven sampling patterns. The authors develop a graph-theoretic approach intended to handle models that can produce power-law distributions of observed entries.

Their analysis translates recovery into a question about complete cascades in random graphs: when can a spreading process reach the whole graph? Using this connection, they establish exact recovery under the Chung-Lu-Vu sampling model. For preferential attachment sampling, they instead hypothesize that the algorithm uses an optimal number of observed entries and provide strong empirical support.

That distinction separates a proved recovery result from a supported conjecture about sample optimality. The authors also report that their method is easier to implement and substantially faster than existing methods. Demonstrations include matrices sampled using common random graph models and the Netflix challenge dataset, connecting the graph-based analysis to practical completion problems.
neurips-2009-matrix-completion-from-powe.tldr: A graph-based matrix completion method proves exact recovery under Chung-Lu-Vu sampling and empirically supports optimal sampling under preferential attachment.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian model of category learning in which beliefs change as observations arrive. The model updates both a category's mean and its variance over time. These quantities describe the category's central tendency and its spread, allowing learning to alter both what is typical and how much variation belongs within the category.

The authors introduce conjugate temporal priors so the updates have closed-form solutions. To represent the spacing effect, they add a prior during temporal updating that expresses a particular learning preference: repetition produces less change, while variation produces more. The way observations unfold over time therefore becomes part of the model's account of learning.

The formulation can be extended to supervised and unsupervised learning with multiple categories. The authors also generalize it to efficient model selection, allowing a decision between explaining observations with one category or several. Together, these developments connect sequential parameter updating with the separate question of how many categories the observations should be assigned to.
neurips-2009-modeling-the-spacing-effect.tldr: A sequential Bayesian category model represents spacing effects through updates that respond less to repetition and more to variation.

paragraphs: Sparse coding proposes that visual cortical activity is optimized so that neural responses are sparse. Testing this idea requires more than observing sparse activity: researchers need reference points for deciding whether the measured sparseness supports an optimization account. This paper uses differences in development and brain state to examine predictions from a sparse coding model.

The authors analyze responses to natural movies in the primary visual cortex. Their data include ferrets at different developmental stages and rats that are awake or under different levels of anesthesia. They examine both population sparseness, concerning activity across neurons, and lifetime sparseness, concerning the responses of individual neurons.

Both measures decrease with visual experience and increase between awake and anesthetized states, contrary to the prediction from the sparse coding model considered. These observations suggest that primary visual cortex representations are not actively optimized to maximize sparseness. The conclusion concerns the proposed optimization principle; observing sparse neural activity by itself would not establish that maximizing sparseness is the system's objective.
neurips-2009-no-evidence-for-active-spar.tldr: Changes in neural sparseness with experience and anesthesia challenge the idea that primary visual cortex actively maximizes sparseness.

paragraphs: This paper addresses learning when high-dimensional data lie on a nonlinear manifold. Its method separates the task into an unsupervised stage that learns a basis and a supervised stage that learns a function. The basis provides anchor points used to describe the local geometry around each data point.

Each point is approximated by a linear combination of nearby anchors. The weights in that combination become the point's local coordinate code. Although the original data geometry is nonlinear, this representation supplies coordinates in which a single global linear function can approximate a high-dimensional nonlinear function. The authors show that the locality of the coding controls approximation quality.

The approach therefore moves a crucial part of the learning problem into the representation. Unsupervised basis learning supplies local reference points, and supervised learning operates on the resulting weights. The stated contribution is a way to turn a difficult nonlinear learning task into global linear learning while overcoming some drawbacks of traditional local methods.
neurips-2009-nonlinear-learning-using-lo.tldr: Local coordinate coding represents data through nearby anchors so a global linear learner can approximate nonlinear functions.

paragraphs: Event coreference resolution groups linguistic references that describe the same event. The grouping may be needed within a single document or across separate documents. This paper approaches that task through unsupervised clustering, developing a sequence of Bayesian nonparametric models for complex linguistic objects rather than relying on supervised training for the clustering task.

The models allow potentially infinite collections of features and categorical outcomes. This is the flexibility emphasized in the proposed representation: the modeling framework does not require those possibilities to be confined to a fixed finite inventory in advance. Features and outcomes are part of the probabilistic treatment of the objects being clustered.

The authors evaluate the models on two corpora, considering both within-document and cross-document event coreference. Every investigated model shows significant improvement over an existing baseline for the task. This supports the usefulness of the proposed modeling approach in the evaluated settings, while keeping the reported comparison tied to the baseline and corpora actually studied.
neurips-2009-nonparametric-bayesian-mode.tldr: Unsupervised Bayesian nonparametric models improve event coreference clustering over an existing baseline on two corpora.

paragraphs: A useful recognition representation should tolerate some changes in an input while retaining distinctions needed to identify it. This is the tension between invariance and selectivity. The paper develops a group-theoretic framework for understanding invariance in a family of hierarchical models, motivated by object recognition and questions about visual cortical representations.

The algebraic perspective provides a concise set of conditions that must hold to establish invariance, together with a constructive procedure for satisfying them. This turns invariance into something that can be analyzed through the model's transformation structure. The framework asks which transformations a hierarchy must support for a desired invariance to follow.

The authors examine specific cases relevant to computer vision and text processing. They identify minimal sets of transformations intrinsic to the hierarchical model that support particular invariances. Such descriptions can guide efficient implementations by making the required transformation structure explicit. The contribution is a mathematical account of how and when invariance can be achieved within the studied model family.
neurips-2009-on-invariance-in-hierarchic.tldr: A group-theoretic framework identifies conditions and transformation sets that support invariance in hierarchical models.

paragraphs: The paper connects two ways of designing investment strategies. One assumes stock returns follow Geometric Brownian Motion, a probabilistic model that is often useful but does not always fit observations. The other takes a worst-case perspective, judging performance against the best fixed portfolio that could have been chosen with hindsight.

That second objective is universal portfolio management. Its benchmark is relative wealth compared with a fixed portfolio, so the guarantee concerns performance against that comparator. The authors design a strategy that remains universal in the worst case while also being capable of exploiting the Geometric Brownian Motion model when its assumptions are useful.

The technical foundation is a set of new and improved regret bounds for online convex optimization with exp-concave losses. Regret expresses the gap between sequential decisions and a comparison strategy. These bounds provide the bridge between using probabilistic structure and retaining a worst-case guarantee, allowing the two perspectives to inform a single investment method.
neurips-2009-on-stochastic-and-worst-cas.tldr: An investment strategy combines worst-case universality with the ability to exploit a useful Geometric Brownian Motion model.

paragraphs: Large image collections mix several kinds of supervision: a few carefully assigned labels, noisier labels inferred from nearby text, and many images without labels. Semi-supervised learning can combine these sources, but the computational cost of the approaches considered becomes impractical at massive scale. This paper develops approximations whose cost grows linearly with the number of images.

The method uses a connection between graph-based and continuous descriptions of data geometry. Eigenvectors of a normalized graph Laplacian converge to eigenfunctions of weighted Laplace-Beltrami operators, and the authors use that relationship to obtain efficient approximations. This mathematical connection supplies the route from an expensive graph-based formulation to a scalable computation.

The system also uses WordNet to share label information across related classes, including classes without manual annotations. The authors apply the resulting algorithm to 80 million images spanning 74 thousand classes. The stated achievement combines computational scale with a mechanism for spreading supervision beyond the categories that have directly labeled examples.
neurips-2009-semi-supervised-learning-in.tldr: Linear-scaling approximations and WordNet label sharing enable semi-supervised learning on 80 million images across 74 thousand classes.

paragraphs: In a hidden Markov model, filtering estimates the current hidden state from observations. This paper asks how that estimate changes when model parameters change, focusing on continuous state and observation spaces. Such sensitivity information is useful when the parameters are unknown and must be learned from an observed sequence.

The authors develop Infinitesimal Perturbation Analysis for the filtering distribution. Their methodology turns an algorithm that estimates the filtering density, including a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm, into one that estimates its gradient. For the resulting particle-based estimator, they prove asymptotic unbiasedness and consistency, with computation growing linearly in the number of particles.

They then derive an estimator for the gradient of the log-likelihood, which can be used by a gradient method to maximize likelihood. This connects sensitivity analysis directly to parameter identification. Numerical experiments illustrate the method. The asymptotic guarantees concern estimator behavior in the relevant limit and do not imply exact gradients from a finite particle approximation.
neurips-2009-sensitivity-analysis-in-hmm.tldr: A sensitivity-analysis method estimates filtering and likelihood gradients in continuous-state HMMs with linear particle complexity.

paragraphs: Sparse estimation seeks an explanation that uses few features from a possibly overcomplete dictionary. Common methods balance data fit against a penalty that acts separately on each coefficient. This paper studies non-factorial priors, which allow the sparsity preference to depend jointly on coefficients, and implements them through efficient, globally convergent reweighted l1 minimization.

For a method derived from sparse Bayesian learning, the authors prove a strong comparison with Lasso in canonical sparse estimation problems. Within that setting, the method cannot do worse, and for every dictionary and sparsity profile there are cases where it does better. This is a scoped theoretical result, despite the underlying objective being highly nonconvex.

A new non-factorial variant has similar properties and further improves performance in empirical tests. The paper also applies reweighted l1 methods to classification, group feature selection, and non-negativity constraints. It derives a reformulation of sparse Bayesian classification that avoids approximation steps and decreases a well-defined objective, providing a clearer optimization foundation for that formulation.
neurips-2009-sparse-estimation-using-gen.tldr: Non-factorial sparse priors yield theoretical advantages over Lasso in canonical problems and support broader estimation through reweighted l1 optimization.

paragraphs: Pointwise mutual information, or PMI, measures association by comparing how often items occur together with what their individual frequencies would suggest. This paper studies how to compute such scores when data arrive as a stream. The motivation comes from space-efficient approximate counting methods that can handle very large vocabularies without maintaining every count exactly.

Moving from counts to association scores raises a separate computational question: what accuracy is achievable online? The authors establish theoretical bounds showing that perfect online PMI computation is impractical. They then describe an algorithm with high expected accuracy, making approximation the basis of the proposed streaming solution.

Experiments on news articles show high accuracy on real-world data. That empirical result complements the theoretical argument: the bounds motivate giving up perfect computation, while the experiments indicate that the proposed approximation can still provide accurate association scores. The contribution is a treatment of PMI itself in the streaming setting, building on the availability of compact approximate counting structures.
neurips-2009-streaming-pointwise-mutual-.tldr: The paper shows why perfect streaming PMI is impractical and presents an approximation with high expected and observed accuracy.

paragraphs: Object detection must handle changes in orientation, shape alignment, and visibility. This paper develops a structured output model that accounts for these factors during both training and prediction. In particular, it explicitly represents partial truncation, allowing examples where only part of an object is visible to participate in the detection formulation.

The model uses large-margin learning with latent variables and slack rescaling. Alignment variables handle small rotations and unequal scaling along different directions, and the same formulation accommodates aspects such as left-facing, right-facing, and frontal views. An explicit truncation mask represents partial visibility. The authors also find that adding a bias term significantly improves the earlier structured regression formulation.

Training and inference are reported to be computationally efficient. On PASCAL VOC 2007, training includes truncated examples, and testing detects objects across scales, alignments, and substantial truncations. The authors identify explicit truncation handling as their most significant performance contribution, showing the value of representing visibility within the model used for both learning and detection.
neurips-2009-structured-output-regressio.tldr: A structured detector models alignment, viewing aspects, and truncation explicitly during both training and inference.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation describes where observations are concentrated without choosing a fixed parametric distribution. Its worst-case performance deteriorates severely as dimension increases. This paper considers a more structured setting: observations occupy a lower-dimensional Riemannian submanifold inside a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, so the number of recorded coordinates can exceed the data's intrinsic dimension.

The authors propose a small modification of kernel density estimation for this setting. Using Riemannian geometry, they prove that the modified estimator is consistent and that its convergence rate depends on the submanifold's intrinsic dimension. The geometric structure is therefore central to the result, determining the dimension that governs statistical convergence.

Empirical results demonstrate behavior predicted by the theory. The significance is that high ambient dimension does not by itself determine the estimator's rate in the studied setting. When the data satisfy the submanifold formulation, the analysis captures their lower-dimensional structure and provides a theoretical basis for density estimation that reflects that structure.
neurips-2009-submanifold-density-estimat.tldr: A modified kernel density estimator has consistency and convergence rates governed by a submanifold's intrinsic dimension.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model's structure means identifying which variables have direct modeled interactions. This paper studies that task for Ising models, which are pairwise Markov random fields with binary variables. The observations are independent samples from the model, and the question is when computationally inexpensive structure-learning methods encounter difficulty.

Through analyses of concrete examples, the authors show that low-complexity algorithms systematically fail when the model develops long-range correlations. Such correlations connect the behavior of variables across the model, making the relationship between observed dependence and local interaction structure harder to resolve in the examined cases. The examples expose limitations that are not obvious from listing the available algorithms.

The failure phenomenon appears related to the Ising model's phase transition, but the authors explicitly state that the two do not coincide. This preserves a distinction between a physical change in model behavior and the observed boundary of algorithmic success. The contribution is evidence connecting correlation structure to learning difficulty, with the phase-transition connection remaining qualified.
neurips-2009-which-graphical-models-are-.tldr: Concrete Ising-model examples link failures of low-complexity structure learning to long-range correlations.

paragraphs: A news photograph and its caption provide related information, but they do not explicitly identify every correspondence. A name must be matched to a face, and an action verb must be associated with a person's body pose. This paper tackles those assignments together, aiming to determine who is pictured and what each person is doing.

The proposed joint model simultaneously learns image-caption correspondences and visual appearance models for the face and pose classes present in the corpus. Learning the assignments and the visual models within one formulation connects the identity and action tasks. The caption supplies names and verbs, while the image supplies the facial and pose evidence to be matched.

Experiments show that the joint face-and-pose model solves the correspondence task better than earlier models that cover faces alone. The learned visual models also recognize people and actions in new images without captions. This demonstrates that the paired image-text corpus can support both annotation of its own examples and recognition when textual assistance is absent.
neurips-2009-whos-doing-what-joint-model.tldr: Jointly learning face, pose, name, and verb correspondences improves image-caption matching and supports recognition in uncaptioned images.
